title: Two filenames that look identical can be different byte strings, and a Linux server will store both
assumption: A filename that looks the same on screen is the same filename on disk.

input.display: "caf\u00e9.txt" encoded as NFC (\u00e9) vs the same visible name encoded as NFD (e + \u0301)
input.description: A filename that arrives in decomposed form (for example, a file that originated on an older Mac HFS+ volume, which stored names in a variant of NFD, or a client that decomposes text) stored verbatim on a Linux server, then looked up by the composed form a different client produced.

what_goes_wrong: A byte-exact filename search for the composed form finds nothing, even though a file with the 'same' visible name exists on disk, because the stored bytes are the decomposed form.
why: NFC and NFD are both valid Unicode encodings of identical visible text, but they are different code-point sequences and therefore different UTF-8 bytes. Linux filesystems like ext4 treat names as opaque bytes with no normalization, so the two forms are two unrelated names: a lookup by one misses the other, and both can coexist in one directory. Mac filesystems behave differently: HFS+ stored names in a variant of NFD, while APFS preserves whichever form it was given but matches names normalization-insensitively, so the same lookup that succeeds on a Mac fails once the file is on a Linux server.
affects: ext4 / most linux filesystems (byte-wise names, no normalization)
macos hfs+ (stores a variant of nfd)
macos apfs (preserves the given form, normalization-insensitive lookup)
any client/server pair that disagrees on normalization form

repros.code:
import unicodedata
nfc = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", "caf\u00e9.txt")
nfd = unicodedata.normalize("NFD", "caf\u00e9.txt")
print(nfc == nfd, len(nfc), len(nfd))
print(nfc.encode("utf-8") == nfd.encode("utf-8"), len(nfc.encode("utf-8")), len(nfd.encode("utf-8")))

fix: Normalize every filename to one form (NFC is the usual choice) at the point it enters your system, before it ever reaches a save or a lookup, so client and server always agree on the byte sequence.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #15: Unicode Normalization Forms
Apple Technical Q&A QA1173: Text Encodings in VFS (HFS+ decomposed names)
Apple File System Guide: FAQ (APFS normalization and case sensitivity)

test_cases.note: A filename-key function should normalize (usually to NFC) so the composed and decomposed spellings map to the same key.
